name: Chromium nicotinate

lead: Chromium nicotinate is trace-mineral chromium bound to niacin, sold in supplements marketed for weight loss, muscle building and blood sugar. People take it for fewer cravings, better nutrient use and a leaner, more muscular look.

Chromium has been proposed to enhance insulin signaling, possibly through a chromium-binding peptide. Reviews of chromium supplements report no reliable evidence for body-weight effects, EFSA found evidence insufficient for body-weight claims, and a trial of chromium nicotinate in type 2 diabetes found no effect on insulin sensitivity. Most research covers picolinate rather than nicotinate.

paras: Taken orally as a daily supplement, often in multivitamin or fat-loss and body-composition stacks, alongside diet and training. Users judge results over weeks to months.

Little evidence of toxicity at typical amounts; rare allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and kidney or liver reports exist, mostly with picolinate. It may interact with medicines, including insulin.

angle.text: Chromium nicotinate is taken for fat loss, muscle gain and blood sugar control, on the idea that chromium improves how the body handles carbohydrate. Trials of chromium forms have measured body composition directly, with mixed results.

lead: Chromium nicotinate (also called niacin-bound chromium or chromium polynicotinate) is a form of trivalent chromium bound to niacin, sold as a dietary supplement alongside chromium picolinate and chromium chloride. People take chromium supplements with the aim of improving how the body handles insulin and carbohydrates, so that they carry less body fat and keep more muscle, which is the physique angle on which it has been marketed to dieters and lifters.[1][2][2]

The idea behind it is that chromium supports insulin signalling. Better insulin sensitivity would mean steadier blood sugar, less fat storage and better nutrient partitioning during a diet or training block. A 2008 review argued that chromium supplements, particularly niacin-bound chromium, may attenuate insulin resistance and lower plasma cholesterol, and it called for nutrigenomic research to identify the genes involved.[2]

Human trials of chromium nicotinate have mostly been done in people with type 2 diabetes or HIV rather than in healthy gym-goers. A randomized trial in 56 overweight people with type 2 diabetes found no change in insulin sensitivity, glycemic control or most lipids over 90 days,[3] while a 16-week trial in 52 people with HIV reported lower insulin resistance and lower total and trunk fat mass.[4] Reviews cited by Wikipedia report that a 2013 Cochrane review and the European Food Safety Authority did not find the data sufficient to support body-weight claims for chromium.[1] Most published work on chromium forms concerns picolinate rather than nicotinate.

paras: Chromium nicotinate is a coordination complex of chromium(III) with nicotinic acid (niacin). It is one of several chromium forms in supplements. Wikipedia states that picolinate is absorbed more efficiently than chloride or nicotinate, and that the biologically active form of chromium is unknown.[1] A 2016 review of organoselenium and chromium(III) complexes lists chromium nicotinate alongside chromium picolinate, histidinate, phenylalaninate and others as complexes that have been studied for low-grade inflammation and type 2 diabetes.[5]

Chromium nicotinate also appears as one ingredient in multi-component weight-management formulas. One randomized, double-blind crossover trial tested HUM5007, a blend that included calcium citrate, green tea extract, ascorbic acid, chromium nicotinate and cholecalciferol, along with 3-acetyl-7-oxo-DHEA, in overweight adults on a calorie-restricted diet, and examined resting metabolic rate. Because the ingredients were combined, that study does not isolate chromium nicotinate.[6]

Chromium products have been marketed for fat loss, muscle gain and improved body composition, including to athletes.[1][2] The insulin-sensitising rationale also underlies their appeal for appetite and carbohydrate-craving control during diets, though trials of that specific outcome with the nicotinate form were not found.

Most investigation has been in glucose control. A 2024 systematic review of randomized trials of chromium in type 2 diabetes included studies of picolinate, chromium yeast, chloride and nicotinate and reported that several trials described possible benefits, with the relationship between supplemental Cr(III) and type 2 diabetes described as controversial.[7]

Wikipedia notes that chromium was once proposed as essential for normal glucose handling, but that this role has not been sufficiently demonstrated, and that EFSA saw no convincing evidence of essentiality.[1] The article describes an early proposal of a "glucose tolerance factor" as the active chromium species, which later research suggested was an artifact of isolation procedures, and describes a chromium-binding peptide, chromodulin, as proposed but not adequately shown to act in living subjects.[1][1]

A 2013 Cochrane review and EFSA are cited by Wikipedia as concluding that evidence did not support firm conclusions on body-weight effects of chromium picolinate, and Wikipedia reports that trials of more than 12 weeks showed at most a small weight loss and no clear effect on muscle growth or fat loss.[1][1] A 1997 trial of chromium picolinate combined with exercise training in obese women is among the older body-composition studies and reported weight gain with supplementation alone.[8] Those findings concern picolinate and not nicotinate.

For nicotinate itself, the two Brazilian randomized trials in people with type 2 diabetes are the main body-composition data. In the 56-person double-blind trial, participants were randomized to placebo, a lower dose or a higher dose of chromium nicotinate for 90 days. There were no differences within or between groups for HOMA-IR, waist circumference, body fat percentage, lean mass percentage or total energy intake, although a small drop of about 1 kg in body weight was seen in the lower-dose group at 90 days.[9] The companion paper on the same design found no differences in fasting glucose, glycosylated hemoglobin, HOMA-IR, total cholesterol or LDL, with a rise in HOMA-beta and HDL.[3]

In the HIV trial, 46 completers took chromium nicotinate or placebo for 16 weeks. The authors reported a fall in HOMA-IR, insulin, triglycerides, total body fat mass (about 17.3 to 16.3 kg) and trunk fat mass, and said it was tolerated without side effects.[4]

Cell and animal work compared chromium forms. A 1992 study in cultured rat muscle cells found that chromium picolinate, but not chromium nicotinate or chloride, increased insulin internalization.[10] A 1997 rat study found that chromium nicotinate and other forms influenced blood pressure and lipid peroxidation in spontaneously hypertensive rats, and followed an earlier study in which oral chromium nicotinate overcame sucrose-induced hypertension in these rats.[11] A 1997 macrophage study compared oxidative stress induced by chromium picolinate and chromium nicotinate in cultured cells.[12] A 2015 mouse study compared chromium methionine with chromium chloride and chromium nicotinate for hypoglycemic activity in alloxan-induced diabetic mice.[13]

A 1995 study found chromosome damage in hamster ovary cells with chromium picolinate.[14] Wikipedia reports that the UK Committee on Mutagenicity later concluded the available data did not support picolinate being mutagenic in vitro, and that the Food Standards Agency withdrew earlier advice to prefer other chromium forms.[1][1]

Wikipedia reports that typical supplemental amounts show little evidence of toxicity, but that adverse effects including allergic reactions, headache, insomnia and irritability have been reported, mostly for picolinate. It describes case reports of kidney failure and liver disease at higher intakes over weeks to months, possible interactions with prescription drugs, and advises against supplementation in pregnancy, while breastfeeding, and for people taking insulin.[1][1]

Regulators have treated chromium claims cautiously. According to Wikipedia, EFSA in 2010 found insufficient evidence for body-weight claims and no convincing evidence that chromium is an essential nutrient, the US FDA in 2005 allowed a qualified health claim about insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes that must state the relationship is highly uncertain, and Health Canada in 2010 approved supplement labelling related to glucose and macronutrient metabolism.[1][1]
Chromium nicotinate is also sold as a component of multi-ingredient fat-burner and "metabolism" products, and trials of such blends are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov.[15]

A randomized trial found chromium nicotinate had no effect on insulin sensitivity, glycemic control or most of the lipid profile in 56 overweight subjects with type 2 diabetes over 90 days.[3] A companion analysis of the same trial design reported no change in waist circumference, body fat percentage or lean mass.[9] A trial of 400 micrograms per day of chromium nicotinate in 52 HIV-infected patients with insulin resistance reported improved insulin resistance and lower fat mass over 16 weeks.[4]

Registered trials include a Phase 3 study of chromium nicotinate in type 2 diabetes (n=57) and a Phase 2 study in HIV patients with metabolic abnormalities (n=52).[16][17] A study of chromium picolinate with exercise in obese women reported weight gain with supplementation alone.[8] A 2024 systematic review examined chromium supplementation in type 2 diabetes across several chromium forms.[7] No published trial testing chromium nicotinate specifically for fat loss or appearance in healthy people was found.

timeline.event: Chromium(III) picolinate is first reported in the chemical literature.[1]
Cell study finds picolinate, but not nicotinate or chloride, increases insulin internalization in rat muscle cells.[10]
Rat and macrophage studies compare chromium nicotinate with picolinate.[11][12]
US FDA allows a qualified chromium picolinate health claim worded as highly uncertain.[1]
EFSA finds insufficient evidence for body-weight claims; HIV trial of chromium nicotinate published.[4][1]
Randomized trial of chromium nicotinate in type 2 diabetes published; Cochrane review of chromium for weight published.[3][1]
Systematic review of chromium supplementation and type 2 diabetes published.[7]
